questions.stem: Which is a typical challenge of the seed stage of the business life cycle?
options: managing a large workforce spread across several states
holding market share against many established competitors
deciding whether to sell the business as sales decline
raising finance for an idea that has no sales record yet
questions.explanation: At the seed stage the idea is unproven, so lenders and investors are cautious and the founder often relies on personal savings. Large workforces and defending market share are problems of later stages.

questions.stem: Before quitting her job, a Rockhampton entrepreneur builds a basic version of her app and asks 50 potential customers to try it. What seed-stage challenge is she addressing?
options: the cost of paying dividends to the business's shareholders each year
uncertainty about whether customers actually want the product
the need to manage the business's rapidly growing sales
the problem of falling sales in a saturated market with many rivals
questions.explanation: Testing a simple prototype with real users reduces the risk of building something nobody wants before committing more money. Growing or falling sales are issues once the business is trading.

questions.stem: A business incubator supports seed-stage businesses mainly by providing:
options: permanent staff who will run the business on the founder's behalf
free legal ownership of the founder's intellectual property
low-cost workspace, mentoring and connections with investors and other founders
a guarantee that the business's products will be bought by the state government
questions.explanation: Incubators help early-stage founders develop their ideas through shared space, advice and networks. They do not guarantee sales or take over running the business.

questions.stem: A founder wants free, reliable information on registering a business, tax obligations and grants available in Queensland. Which source is most appropriate?
options: a customer survey asking which colour the logo should be
government business information websites such as Business Queensland
an anonymous social media post from someone claiming to be an expert
a competitor that already sells a similar product in the same town
questions.explanation: Government business information services provide authoritative, free guidance on registration, tax, licences and support programs. Anonymous posts may be inaccurate, and competitors are unlikely to help.

questions.stem: Why might a seed-stage entrepreneur seek advice from an accountant before launching?
options: to design the product's packaging and choose its brand colours and logo
to recruit and train the business's first sales staff
to register the product as a patent with IP Australia
to understand start-up costs, cash flow, tax and the best legal structure
questions.explanation: Accountants advise on financial planning, tax obligations and structure, which reduces costly mistakes early. Branding and recruitment are other areas, and patent applications are usually prepared with a patent attorney.

questions.stem: Incremental innovation is:
options: a completely new technology that creates an entirely new market
a simpler, cheaper offering that eventually displaces market leaders
a process of copying a competitor's product without any changes
a small improvement to an existing product, service or process
questions.explanation: Incremental innovation makes gradual improvements, such as a longer-lasting battery in a familiar device. A completely new technology is radical innovation, and a cheaper offering that displaces leaders is disruptive innovation.

questions.stem: Disruptive innovation describes an offering that:
options: starts with a simpler or cheaper product for overlooked customers and later displaces established firms
makes a small improvement to an existing product for the business's current customers and keeps prices stable
is produced by an established market leader to protect its existing products
is protected by a patent so that no competitor can enter the market at all
questions.explanation: Disruptive innovations often begin at the low end of a market or in a new market that leaders ignore, then improve until they draw mainstream customers away. Small improvements for existing customers are incremental.

questions.stem: A drink company releases its best-selling juice in a new mango flavour and a recyclable bottle. Which type of innovation is this?
options: disruptive innovation
no innovation
incremental innovation
radical innovation
questions.explanation: A new flavour and better packaging improve an existing product without changing the market, which is incremental. Radical innovation involves a breakthrough that creates something fundamentally new.

questions.stem: A start-up launches a cheap, easy app that lets small businesses do their own bookkeeping. At first established accounting firms ignore it, but over time it wins many of their clients. Which type of innovation is this?
options: disruptive innovation
incremental innovation
radical innovation
a registered design
questions.explanation: The app began as a simple, low-cost option for an overlooked segment and grew to take customers from incumbents, the pattern of disruptive innovation. It is not a small improvement to the firms' own services.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates radical innovation?
options: a phone manufacturer adding a slightly better camera and a larger battery to this year's model
a bakery adding a gluten-free version of its most popular bread
a supermarket offering longer opening hours on public holidays
the first commercially available technology that changes how a product works at a fundamental level
questions.explanation: Radical innovation is a breakthrough based on new technology or knowledge, often creating new markets. A better camera or a new bread variety is incremental, and longer hours is a change in service, not a technological breakthrough.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes radical from disruptive innovation?
options: radical innovation always starts at the low end of a market; disruptive innovation never affects any established firms
radical innovation is a small change to an existing product; disruptive innovation is a completely new invention
radical and disruptive innovation are identical terms for the same type of innovation
radical innovation is defined by a technological breakthrough; disruptive innovation by how it overturns existing markets
questions.explanation: Radical describes the scale of the technological change, while disruptive describes the market effect of displacing incumbents, often with a simpler product. An innovation can be one without being the other.

questions.stem: Which correctly lists Maslow's hierarchy of needs from the base upwards?
options: physiological, esteem, safety, self-actualisation, love and belonging
physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualisation
safety, physiological, esteem, love and belonging, self-actualisation
self-actualisation, esteem, love and belonging, safety, physiological
questions.explanation: Maslow placed basic physiological needs at the base, followed by safety, love and belonging, esteem and, at the top, self-actualisation. Lower needs generally must be met before higher ones motivate behaviour.

questions.stem: A business idea for a home security camera system mainly appeals to which level of Maslow's hierarchy?
options: esteem
self-actualisation
physiological
safety
questions.explanation: Security systems help people feel protected from harm, which is a safety need. Esteem needs relate to status and recognition, and physiological needs to food, water and shelter.

questions.stem: A luxury watch brand promotes its products as a symbol of success and status. Which level of Maslow's hierarchy is it targeting?
options: love and belonging
physiological
esteem
safety
questions.explanation: Status, respect and recognition are esteem needs. The watch is not mainly bought for safety or basic survival.

questions.stem: A business offers online courses that help adults pursue a lifelong passion, such as painting or composing music. Which level of Maslow's hierarchy does this idea mainly meet?
options: safety
physiological
love and belonging
self-actualisation
questions.explanation: Self-actualisation is about reaching one's potential and personal growth, which matches pursuing creative passions. Joining a community could add belonging, but the main appeal is personal fulfilment.

questions.stem: An entrepreneur already earns a secure income but starts a business mainly to prove she can build something of her own and fulfil her potential. According to Maslow, what is her main motive?
options: safety needs, as she wants to protect her current job
love and belonging, as she wants to join a team at work
self-actualisation, as her lower needs are already met
physiological needs, as she needs money to buy food
questions.explanation: With income and security already in place, her motivation sits at the top of the hierarchy: achieving her potential. Physiological and safety needs are already satisfied, so they are not driving the decision.

questions.stem: In the SCAMPER technique, the letters stand for:
options: substitute, compete, adapt, manufacture, promote, export, retail
substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to another use, eliminate, reverse
sell, create, advertise, market, price, evaluate, research
strategy, competition, analysis, mission, planning, economics, risk
questions.explanation: SCAMPER prompts new ideas by asking how an existing product or process could be substituted, combined, adapted, modified, put to another use, have parts eliminated, or be reversed or rearranged.

questions.stem: A café starts offering a coffee and a bike repair while you wait, in the same shop. Which SCAMPER prompt does this idea best reflect?
options: reverse
substitute
combine
eliminate
questions.explanation: Joining two different offerings into one business is the combine prompt. Eliminate would remove a feature, and substitute would replace one part with another.

questions.stem: A furniture company replaces timber in its outdoor chairs with recycled plastic from ocean waste. Which SCAMPER prompt is this?
options: reverse
substitute
combine
put to another use
questions.explanation: Swapping one material for another is substitution. Putting to another use would find a new purpose for the existing product, rather than changing what it is made from.

questions.stem: A business sells used coffee grounds from cafés to gardeners as fertiliser. Which SCAMPER prompt does this best reflect?
options: eliminate
adapt
put to another use
modify
questions.explanation: Finding a new purpose for an existing item, here a waste product, is the put to another use prompt. Modify would change the product's size, shape or features.

questions.stem: A gym removes its front desk, staff and contracts, offering 24-hour app-based entry at a much lower monthly price. Which SCAMPER prompt best describes the idea, and how could it be screened?
options: eliminate; screen it by checking demand and whether the lower price still covers costs
combine; screen it by adding as many extra services as possible before the launch date
reverse; screen it by copying the busiest competitor's prices exactly
substitute; screen it by registering the name before researching any customers
questions.explanation: Removing features to simplify the service and cut costs is the eliminate prompt. Ideas are screened by testing demand, costs and fit with goals before investing heavily.

questions.stem: In a PEST analysis, the factors examined are:
options: price, efficiency, strategy and tactics
planning, evaluating, selling and testing
political, economic, sociocultural and technological
product, environment, staff and training
questions.explanation: PEST is a macro environment tool covering political, economic, sociocultural and technological factors. It focuses on external forces the business cannot control.

questions.stem: In a PEST analysis for an electric bike hire idea in Brisbane, a council plan to build more separated bike lanes belongs under:
options: economic
sociocultural
technological
political
questions.explanation: Government decisions, policies and spending are political factors. Rising consumer incomes would be economic, and changing attitudes to cycling would be sociocultural.

questions.stem: In the same PEST analysis, longer-lasting and cheaper batteries belong under:
options: economic
sociocultural
technological
political
questions.explanation: Advances in products and processes are technological factors. Cheaper batteries also affect costs, but the change itself arises from technology.

questions.stem: A PEST analysis for a home-cooked meal delivery idea shows more people working from home and rising household incomes, but higher fuel prices. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: demand looks favourable, but delivery costs need managing, for example with efficient routes
the idea should be abandoned, because any single negative factor makes a business idea unviable
fuel prices are an internal weakness, so they belong in a SWOT rather than PEST
the trends cancel each other out, so they have no implication for the idea
questions.explanation: Interpreting the trends together shows positive sociocultural and economic demand factors alongside a cost pressure that the plan must address. One negative factor does not make an idea unviable, and fuel prices are an external factor.

questions.stem: A point of difference is:
options: a feature that makes a business's offering stand out from competitors in customers' eyes
the gap between a product's selling price and its cost price, per unit sold
the difference between a business's strengths and its weaknesses
the distance between a business and its nearest competitor
questions.explanation: A point of difference is what makes customers choose one business over its rivals, such as quality, service or a unique feature. The gap between price and cost is the profit margin.

questions.stem: Three ice-cream shops operate on the same Noosa street. A new entrant plans to make all its flavours from native Queensland fruits. What is the main purpose of this?
options: to avoid any need for marketing or promotion
to prevent the other shops from selling ice-cream
to differentiate the business so it does not have to compete on price alone
to reduce the business's costs below those of every rival shop on the street
questions.explanation: Differentiation gives customers a reason to choose the new shop in a crowded market. It may raise costs rather than lower them, and the business still needs to promote its point of difference.

questions.stem: A registered design protects:
options: the new and distinctive visual appearance of a product, such as its shape
how an invention works and the new technology behind it
a brand name, logo or slogan used to identify a business's products to customers
original written, musical and artistic works automatically
questions.explanation: Registered designs protect how a product looks. How an invention works is protected by a patent, brands by trade marks, and original creative works by copyright.

questions.stem: A Townsville inventor creates a new device that keeps solar panels clean without water. Which form of intellectual property protects how the device works?
options: a patent
a trade mark
a registered design
a business name registration
questions.explanation: A patent protects new, inventive devices, substances, methods or processes and how they work. A registered design protects only appearance, and a trade mark protects branding.

questions.stem: How long can a registered trade mark in Australia last?
options: five years, after which it can never be renewed
twenty years, after which anyone may use the brand
only while the original owner is alive
ten years, renewable indefinitely while the fees are paid
questions.explanation: A registered trade mark lasts ten years and can be renewed every ten years without limit. A standard patent, by contrast, generally lasts up to twenty years and cannot be renewed.

questions.stem: A start-up has invented a new kind of water bottle with a unique filter system and an eye-catching shape, sold under the name 'PureFlow'. Which combination of protection is most complete?
options: a patent for the filter, a registered design for the shape and a trade mark for the name
a trade mark for the filter, a patent for the shape and a registered design for the name
copyright for the filter and the shape, and a business name registration for 'PureFlow'
a single patent, which automatically protects the filter, the shape and the name
questions.explanation: Each form of IP protects something different: patents protect how inventions work, registered designs protect appearance and trade marks protect brand identifiers. Business name registration gives no ownership rights over a name.

questions.stem: A founder evaluates two ideas using the business criteria. Idea A has strong customer interest but high costs per unit; Idea B is cheap to produce but has many established rivals. Which recommendation best uses the criteria?
options: choose A, because customer interest is the only criterion that matters in deciding viability
choose B, because the cheaper idea is always the more viable one, regardless of how strong the competition is
reject both, because any idea with a weakness against one criterion cannot proceed to start-up
weigh A's stakeholder appeal against its efficiency, and B's efficiency against its weak competitiveness, before choosing
questions.explanation: A sound evaluation compares each idea across competitiveness, effectiveness, efficiency and stakeholder satisfaction, weighing strengths against weaknesses. No single criterion decides viability, and an idea with weaknesses may still be worth pursuing.
